report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.title: Exploring the changeability of transdiagnostic symptom interactions during treatment using longitudinal network models
table.research_questions: How do core symptoms of depression and anxiety interact in patients with depression, and how do these symptom interactions change during treatment? We hypothesize substantial interactions between the core symptoms of depression and anxiety in the baseline network. Additionally, consistent with network theory (Borsboom, 2017), we expect the number and intensity of these symptom interactions to decrease through psychological treatment.
table.datasets_used:
We will utilize data from a monocentric, rater-blinded, prospective, parallel-group, block-RCT (https://doi.org/10.1186/s12888-020-02880-x) that compared the effects of three different psychological treatments for depression in an inpatient and day clinic setting. In this trial, N = 290 patients with a primary diagnosis of major depressive disorder (MDD) underwent 7 weeks of treatment, randomized to one of three interventions: 1) schema therapy, 2) cognitive-behavioral therapy, or 3) individual supportive therapy. Therapy included up to 14 individual and 14 group sessions, including concomitant care and no restriction on concurrent antidepressant medication. 

Depressive symptoms, the primary outcome, as well as other psychiatric, behavioral, cognitive, psychophysiological, and biological parameters were measured at multiple timepoints: before treatment, during the 7-week treatment period, immediately after treatment, and at follow-ups, conducted after 6, 24, and 48 months. Self-reported symptoms of depression and anxiety were reported using the Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II) and the Brief Symptom Inventory (BSI). These assessments were conducted at baseline (t0), weekly during and after treatment (t1–t7), and at follow-up timepoints. For the current analysis, only the equidistant BSI measurements (t0-t7) are utilized.

table.manipulated_variables: In this study, the manipulated variable is the treatment group. Patients meeting the inclusion criteria were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: schema therapy, cognitive behavioral therapy, or individual supportive therapy.
table.measured_variables:
The variables used in this analysis represent the core symptoms of depression and anxiety, assessed weekly by the Brief Symptom Inventory (BSI). According to the ICD-10 diagnostic criteria, the core symptoms for major depressive disorder (MDD) involve (1) depressed mood, (2) loss of interest or pleasure, and (3) decrease in activity or fatigue; whereas the core symptoms of generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) include (1) worry, nervousness, fear, or dread, (2) physical tension, and (3) autonomic arousal (such as sweating, dizziness, difficulty breathing, and epigastric discomfort). For this analysis, only BSI-items that correspond to these core symptoms of MDD and GAD will be included. Thus, we propose the following BSI item to ICD-10 criteria to mapping:

- depressed mood – item 17 (feeling blue)
- loss of interest – item 18 (feeling no interest in things)
- decrease in activity – item 15 (feeling blocked in getting things done)
- nervousness – item 1 (nervousness or shakiness inside)
- physical tension – item 38 (feeling tense or keyed up) and item 49 (feeling so restless you 
  couldn’t sit still)
- autonomic arousal – item 2 (faintness or dizziness), item 23 (nausea or upset stomach), item 
  29 (trouble getting your breath), and item 30 (hot or cold spells). 

To ensure the best possible alignment with ICD-10 criteria, this mapping is not limited to items from the BSI’s depression and anxiety subscales. If multiple items correspond equally well to a diagnostic criterion, the criterion will be considered present if any of the associated items are marked as present.
table.missing_data_handling: Of the 290 patients recruited, 206 completed the allocated 7-week treatment. Dropout reasons involved early discharge (n = 45), reported overload (n = 13), missed > 6 sessions (n = 7), and other reasons (n = 19). Of the 2320 planned BSI assessments (8 measurement points x 290 patients), n = 462 (19.91%) were entirely missing. Patients will be included if they report data for at least one measurement point. Missing values will not be imputed.
table.unit_of_analysis: The current analysis operates on a patient-by-week level, accounting for potential effects of the treatment group. All available data from the BSI assessments (i.e., baseline assessment and weekly assessments during 7-week treatment) will be included in the analysis. BSI scores are analyzed on a symptom level; no depression or anxiety sum scores are calculated.

table.prior_knowledge: Across treatment groups, depressive symptoms significantly decreased during therapy, indicating that treatment was effective in general. Thus, we expect to find corresponding changes in symptom network structures. CBT was found to be slightly superior to ST and IST at the end of treatment, but effects partially disappeared by follow-up. Thus, we do not propose specific hypotheses regarding treatment group effects but instead plan to evaluate them based on the empirical model fit (see Section Statistical Model). All other previous examinations were not related to the current research questions.
table.statistical_tests:
BSI item responses will be dichotomized in the corresponding symptom being present (item score of 2 – “moderately”, 3 – “quite a bit”, or 4 – “extremely”) or not present (item score of 0 – “not at all”, or 1 – “a little bit”). The planned analysis comprises 1) model development and 2) network construction based on estimated coefficients from the best-fitting model.

1) MODEL DEVELOPMENT:
For each of the 6 core symptoms, a Bayesian multilevel logistic regression model will be fitted. Specifically, each model will predict the presence of a symptom at timepoint t based on the presence of that symptom and all other symptoms at the previous timepoint (t-1, i.e., lagged symptoms). Additionally, a linear interaction term between the lagged symptom (at t-1) and timepoint (t) will be included to capture linear changes in symptom interactions over the course of therapy. 

Several variations of this model will be estimated:

1. Random Intercept Model: Includes only random intercepts, allowing intercepts to vary between persons. The model provides an estimate for the mean changes in symptom interactions during therapy.

2. Random Baseline Symptom Association Model: Includes random effects for the intercept and the lagged-symptom presence (i.e., the presence of symptoms at 𝑡−1), allowing intercepts and temporal symptom associations to vary between persons. 

3. Random Baseline & Change Symptom Association Model: Includes random effects for all predictors (i.e., the presence of symptoms at 𝑡−1 and their interaction with timepoint), allowing all intercepts and symptom associations and their change vary between persons. As this model allows change rates to be person-specific, it facilitates the construction of time-variant patient-specific networks.

For all models, data from all treatment groups are analyzed simultaneously. To empirically identify the best-fitting model, two versions are estimated, respectively: (a) a sparse model without differentiation between treatment groups and (b) a full model that includes the treatment effect as an additional fixed effect interaction term. In the full model, the treatment effect is assessed through a three-way interaction between lagged symptoms, timepoint, and treatment group. Consequently, each of the three models described above is estimated in both (a) and (b) versions.

For all parameters, weakly informative priors are used: Normal(0,3) for population intercept and population slopes (fixed effects) and HalfCauchy(3) for the standard deviations of the population effect (random effects). Convergence will be checked using trace plots and the Gelman-Rubin potential scale reduction statistic. If all models provide estimable solutions, model fit will be evaluated using Watanabe-Akaike Information Criterion (WAIC), R², and Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOO). The model yielding the best fit will be selected for subsequent network construction. Additionally, for the final model, each symptom will be evaluated by comparing observed and predicted symptom frequencies over time.

2) NETWORK CONSTRUCTION: 
Using the coefficient estimates from the superior model identified in step 1, symptom networks will be constructed for each of the eight timepoints (pre-treatment baseline and weekly assessments during the 7-week treatment period). If a full model version provides the best fit, symptom networks will be constructed for each timepoint and treatment group. The regression coefficients describing the direction and strength of the longitudinal associations between symptoms will serve as edge weights in the network. The robustness of all edges will be evaluated using 95% credibility intervals. To evaluate network structure, average raw strength, average absolute strength, instrength, outstrength, out-expected influence, and in-expected influence metrics for each node (symptom) are to be assessed. These metrics will be compared across symptoms, timepoints, and treatment groups (if applicable) to evaluate changes during therapy.
table.assumption_violation_model_non_convergen: If none of the above stated models provides estimable solutions, a cross-lagged network model will be applied (see Wysocki et al., 2022). This approach allows for evaluating change in symptom interactions between core symptoms of depression and anxiety but does not enable person-specific networks to be estimated.
table.exploratory_analyses:
1. Analysis of Person-Specific Networks: If Model 3 will show the best model fit, person-specific networks will be constructed to explore whether symptom interactions and their changes during treatment differ between individuals. 

2. Network Structure and Treatment Response: If Model 3 demonstrates the best fit, we will exploratorily investigate the relationship between symptom network structure and treatment response. Specifically, depression severity (assessed using the BDI-II) at the end of treatment and at follow-up timepoints will be regressed on parameters describing the structure of person-specific networks at baseline (t0) and their changes during treatment, while accounting for baseline and end of treatment symptom severity. This analysis will follow the machine learning approach outlined by Schumacher et al. (2024).

text.text: Question: Does network theory's prediction that successful treatment weakens symptom interactions generalize to short, intensive treatment and transdiagnostic symptom networks?

Findings: In this secondary analysis of a randomized clinical trial including 288 adults, we found little evidence of systematic change in temporal symptom interactions but some indication of a shift toward healthier network-implied symptom dynamics over 7 weeks of treatment.

Meaning: Short-term symptom improvement may occur without detectable weakening of symptom interactions, highlighting the need to evaluate general activation tendency and specific network features as additional indicators of treatment-related change.
exploratory network-implied stability landscapes indicated a system shift toward lower-symptom states.
Conclusions and Relevance.
These findings provide limited support for the prediction that successful treatment reduces global connectivity in short, intensive treatment settings.

In such settings, treatment-related change in symptom severity may be reflected in a reduction in general likelihood of symptom occurrence, but not necessarily in changes in symptom interactions, raising questions about long-term vulnerability.
On the other hand, global symptom connectivity alone may not sufficiently characterize a healthy symptom system, and the role of specific symptom interactions warrants further investigation.

text.text: The network theory of mental disorders 1 conceptualizes psychopathology as a system of causally interacting symptoms. 1, 2 When symptom interactions are numerous or strong, symptoms may mutually reinforce one another and stabilize a disordered state; when interactions are fewer or weaker, the system may be less self-sustaining and more compatible with healthy functioning. 1, 3 The network theory has motivated various proposals for targeted and personalized treatment by identifying symptoms and symptom interactions that are expected to maintain psychopathology. [4] [5] [6] [7] [8] These include network-supported case conceptualization 7 and personalized interventions that use person-specific networks to select and prioritize treatment targets and match them to evidence-based treatment modules. 4, [8] [9] [10] Such applications rely on a central treatment-related premise of the network theory: if strong symptom interactions are central to maintaining psychopathology, they should be modifiable through treatment.

text.text: Specifically, successful treatment should not only reduce symptom severity but also alter the pattern and reduce the strength of symptom interactions, potentially shifting the system toward a less connected, healthier state. 1, 11 Empirical support for this prediction is needed before network structure can confidently guide intervention targets. 12 However, empirical tests of these treatment-related propositions remain scarce.

text.text: Intensive longitudinal studies comparing preand post-treatment periods provide a first indication but have yielded mixed findings. [19] [20] [21] Two studies repeatedly assessed network structure throughout treatment, 12, 22 although only one examined changes in overall connectivity. 22 Using a time-varying longitudinal network model, Schumacher et al. 12 provided the most direct test during 1 year of outpatient psychotherapy for chronic depression.

text.text: Specific symptom interactions changed across treatment conditions and individuals.
However, contrary to network theory's prediction, absolute connectivity did not decrease, partly because negative (inhibitory) interactions emerged in successful treatment.

To further test the validity of the network theory's treatment-related implications, additional evidence is crucial, particularly regarding their generalizability across settings, timescales, and symptoms.

As prior work 12 focused on long-term outpatient psychotherapy for chronic depression, short but intensive inpatient or day-clinic treatment provides an informative complementary test across a compressed timescale.

text.text: Given the frequent co-occurrence of depression and anxiety, 23, 24 a transdiagnostic perspective is particularly relevant in such highly comorbid populations. 25, 26 A key strength of the network framework is that symptoms across diagnostic domains can be modeled within the same system, making it particularly suited to transdiagnostic questions. 1, 27, 28 In this preregistered secondary analysis, we apply a time-varying longitudinal network model 12 to test whether network structure changes systematically during intensive short-term treatment, jointly evaluating anxiety and depression symptoms. 1, 11 Following the network theory, we hypothesize that successful treatment corresponds to reduced overall connectivity (ie, fewer and/or weaker symptom interactions).

text.text: All participants provided written informed consent prior to enrollment.

Details on trial procedures and primary outcomes are reported elsewhere. 29, 30 Patients aged 18 to 75 years were recruited between September 2017 and October 2020, and the present secondary analysis was conducted between January 2025 and May 2026.

text.text: Eligible participants had a primary diagnosis of moderate to severe depression without psychotic symptoms.

Participants received 7 weeks of inpatient or day-clinic treatment and were randomized to schema therapy (ST), cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), or individual supportive therapy (IST) as a nonspecific active control intervention.
Each condition included up to two individual and two group sessions per week, supplemented by concomitant care (eg, ergotherapy and relaxation training).
Medication was permitted and managed as clinically indicated.
This secondary analysis included participants who met the inclusion criteria and contributed at least two symptom assessments to the network analysis, resulting in a final sample of N = 288 patients.
Participants were aged 19 to 74 years (M = 43.6, SD = 13.6), and 55.6% identified as female.

The sample exhibited high rates of comorbidity, including anxiety (62.5%), substance use (27.6%), and somatoform disorders (23.5%; based on n = 272 with available M-CIDI data). 31 Participants attended a mean of 20.31 sessions over the 7-week period and completed on average 6.45 of 8 weekly assessments (19.4% of assessment occasions fully missing).

Network Model: To examine whether symptom interactions changed during treatment, we used a time-varying multilevel vector autoregressive (VAR) model. 12 For each symptom, presence at timepoint t is predicted by its own and all other symptoms at t-1 (ie, lagged symptoms) and by the interaction between each lagged symptom and treatment week, allowing temporal interactions to change linearly across treatment.

text.text: This framework allows for the explicit modeling of change in symptom interactions over time.
A random intercept captured betweenperson differences in baseline symptom presence.
This model was selected over candidate models allowing differential treatment effects and person-specific symptom interactions or change rates based on model fit.

As a sensitivity analysis, we added time as a main effect to the final model to account for overall temporal trends in symptom probabilities that are not captured through changes in temporal interactions alone.
Details on all model specifications, estimation procedures, and model comparisons are provided in the eMethods and eTables 2 and 3 in the Supplement.

We used Bayesian multilevel logistic regression with Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling, fitting one model per symptom in R (version 4.4.2) 37 using brms (version 2.22.0). 38 Convergence was assessed using trace plots and the Gelman-Rubin statistic 39 , and model performance was evaluated for each symptom via Bayesian pseudo-R² and by comparing predicted with observed symptom frequencies across timepoints.

text.text: Posterior estimates were used to derive one symptom network for each treatment week (t0-t7).
Connectivity indices were based on cross-lagged edges only, excluding autoregressive effects to capture connectivity between symptoms.

Global connectivity was summarized using mean absolute strength (mean of all edge weights regardless of valence) and mean raw strength (mean of signed associations, allowing positive and negative edges to cancel each other out).
Node-specific in-and out-strength and in-and out-expected influence summarized incoming and outgoing absolute and signed edge weights, respectively.
These node-specific metrics reflect the relative influence a symptom receives from or exerts on other symptoms over time.

text.text: We explored simulation-based stability landscapes to examine the stability of different mental health states which were defined by the number of present symptoms. 40, 41 Stability landscapes characterize the network-implied symptom dynamics and can identify attractor states toward which the system most strongly leans. 42 Clinically, they can complement connectivity measures by indicating whether treatment-related changes in network structure are accompanied by a shift toward healthier symptom dynamics, ie, more stable states of few present symptoms (eMethods in the Supplement).

text.text: The final model allowed all symptom interactions to change linearly over time, with effects pooled across individuals and treatment arms.
It explained about half of the variation in symptom presence during treatment, with Bayesian pseudo-R² values ranging from 0.43 to 0.54 across symptoms.

Model-predicted symptom frequencies captured the observed decline in symptom presence across treatment well, although reductions tended to be slightly overestimated toward the end of treatment (eFigure 1 in the Supplement).
Thus, overall model fit was good, and the model reproduced broad mean-level symptom improvement by entirely modeling change through lagged symptom interactions.
Figure 1 visualizes the estimated temporal symptom networks at baseline (A), mid-treatment (B), and end of treatment (C); networks for all 8 timepoints are shown in eFigure 3 in the Supplement.

text.text: At baseline, 12 of 36 lagged effects (6/6 autoregressive; 6/30 cross-lagged) were substantial (ie, their 95% credibility intervals did not include 0) compared with 20 of 36 at mid-treatment (6/6; 14/30) and 7 of 36 after the 7-week treatment (3/6; 4/30).
All substantial edges were positive.
Estimated changes in symptom interactions were small.
Of 36 change rates, point estimates suggested decreasing associations over time for 21 edges, essentially no change for 4, and increasing associations for 11 (eTable 4 in the Supplement).
However, only 3 change rates were substantial, ie, supported with 95% credibility (Figure 1).
text.formatted: However, only 3 change rates were substantial, ie, supported with 95% credibility (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: The autoregressive effects of arousal and loss of interest became less strongly self-predictive over time (β arousal = -0.19; 95% CI, -0.37 to -0.02; β loss of interest = -0.23; 95% CI, -0.42 to -0.03), whereas the crosslagged effect from arousal to physical tension increased (β = 0.16; 95% CI, 0.01 to 0.30).
Consistent with the limited evidence for changing symptom interactions through treatment, global network metrics based on cross-lagged effects showed only small shifts over time.

Mean absolute strength of temporal symptom associations declined from 0.55 (95% CI, 0.47-0.64) at treatment start to 0.46 (95% CI, 0.38-0.54) at treatment end, but overlapping credibility intervals indicate no robust effect (Figure 2A).

text.text: Mean raw strength of temporal symptom associations showed a similar pattern, decreasing from 0.45 (95% CI, 0.38-0.51) to 0.37 (95% CI, 0.30-0.43; Figure 2B).

text.text: Node-specific metrics (in-strength, out-strength, in-/outexpected influence) likewise remained largely stable (eFigure 5 in the Supplement).
Exploratory inspection suggested qualitative shifts in a small set of dyadic feedback patterns.

Several bidirectional associations evident at baseline (eg, depressed mood ↔ loss of interest; loss of interest ↔ decreased activity; nervousness ↔ physical tension) were not present with 95% certainty posttreatment (Figure 1A and C).

text.text: Including time as a main effect yielded similar overall fit (Bayesian pseudo-R², 0.43-0.55) and a comparable pattern of symptom decline, with slight overestimation of improvement toward treatment end (eFigure 2 in the Supplement).
Time showed a substantial main effect for 3 of 6 symptoms, all indicating a decreasing probability of symptom presence over time.
Two of the 3 change rates identified in the primary model (autoregressive changes for loss of interest and autonomic arousal) were no longer supported by 95% credibility (eTable 5; eFigure 4).
Exploratory stability landscape analyses showed an apparent shift toward lowersymptom states during treatment (Figure 3).

text.text: At treatment start, states with 3 to 4 present symptoms were most likely, whereas the symptom network tended toward 1 to 2 present symptoms at mid-treatment and 0 to 1 active symptoms at treatment end.
However, the end-oftreatment basin was relatively shallow, indicating only a weak preference for the attractor state of few symptoms present.
A similar qualitative shift emerged in the sensitivity analysis including time as a main effect (eFigure 6 in the Supplement).
Thus, despite limited evidence for changes in network structure, the landscapes suggested a shift toward healthier system configurations over treatment.

In this preregistered secondary analysis of a 7-week inpatient/day-clinic randomized controlled trial for depression, 29, 30 we examined the treatment-related implications of the network theory across settings, timescales, and symptoms.

text.text: Despite substantial symptom improvement, 30 we found little evidence of systematic change in temporal symptom interactions or reduced network connectivity, providing limited support for the prediction that successful treatment should lead to a less connected symptom network.

text.text: Most lagged effects remained stable in magnitude and valence, and unlike Schumacher et al, 12 no negative (ie, inhibitory) cross-lagged interactions emerged.

text.text: Nevertheless, model-predicted symptom frequencies captured the overall decline in symptom presence well, and exploratory stability landscapes shifted toward healthier, lower-symptom states by treatment end.
This apparent dissociation raises the question of how treatment-related change was represented in our models.

In the primary model, systematic change through treatment could enter only through changing symptom interactions, and even small and uncertain changes (most point estimates differed from the null and tended toward decreases) allowed the model to reproduce the symptom decline well.

The sensitivity model fitted similarly when each symptom's general activation tendency was additionally allowed to change over time, making activation tendency a potentially relevant additional indicator of change.

We use this term to denote the likelihood of symptom occurrence that is not explained by symptom interactions, conceptually opposite to its "threshold". 43 Lower activation tendency can be interpreted as greater resilience to activation, requiring stronger input from the system or external field. 42, 43 Observed symptom presence is the realized state at a specific timepoint and is strongly influenced, but not determined, by activation tendency.

text.text: Intensive inpatient treatment may rapidly reduce symptom occurrence in acutely ill patients, whereas changes in maintaining symptom interactions may lag behind and require longer periods of (re-)learning and consolidation.
Such changes may become apparent only with longer observation or more sustained treatment, including subsequent outpatient care.

Continued care after discharge is crucial for maintaining treatment gains and reducing relapse risk, 49 and clinical guidelines recommend continuation of psychological treatment and transition to outpatient care. [50] [51] [52] [53] Repeated network assessments beyond discharge and across treatment settings differing in duration and intensity could help distinguish these explanations.

text.text: More importantly, the distinction between symptom interactions and general activation tendency may matter for the durability of symptom relief.

Our findings may resemble a "silent disorder," in which symptoms are currently less active while pathways of mutual reinforcement persist, potentially leaving the system vulnerable to reactivation under external stress. 2, 54 Whether lower activation tendency reflects sustained recovery or primarily transient symptom relief with remaining relapse risk, and whether changes in symptom interactions carry different prognostic information, should be tested against follow-up outcomes.

text.text: Prior work showed incremental prognostic value of symptom interaction changes beyond changes in symptom activation tendency. 55 In contrast, our results might suggest that a healthier symptom system may need to be characterized more broadly than by reduced connectivity alone.

text.text: Lower activation tendencies may mark meaningful improvement even when interactions change little, highlighting the need to distinguish activation tendency, symptom interactions, and symptom severity when evaluating treatment success.
Future models should estimate these components jointly and examine their independent and incremental value for evaluating treatment success.
Network theory may also need greater specificity about which structural properties should change with successful treatment.

Although the theory predicts weaker symptom interactions and lower overall connectivity with successful treatment, 1, 11 global connectivity did not substantially decline despite marked symptom improvement.

text.text: Short-term improvement may therefore not require a detectable reduction in global connectivity, or global metrics may be too coarse to capture clinically relevant change.

More fine-grained indicators, including changes in feedback loops, autoregressive dynamics, or the stability of symptom states, may be informative. 3, [40] [41] [42] [43] 56 Limitations Several limitations warrant consideration.

text.text: First, despite theoretical emphasis on individual-level symptom dynamics, 1, 11 the best-fitting model pooled symptom interactions and change rates across participants and treatment arms.

text.text: Although supported by model fit indices and similar estimates across alternative specifications, group-level averages may obscure clinically relevant heterogeneity 57 and limit inference about person-specific mechanisms of change.

text.text: Second, weekly assessments may have been insensitive to faster symptom dynamics.
With several therapy sessions per week, each interval spanned multiple therapeutic events, so session-to-session changes could be averaged over or missed.
Whether this underestimated treatment-related change depends on the timescale of interaction dynamics, which remains insufficiently understood.

Third, although clinically relevant in a highly comorbid sample, the transdiagnostic inclusion of depression and anxiety symptoms may limit comparability with prior depression-specific networks. 12 Restricting each disorder to 3 core symptoms ensured estimability 17 but may have captured only part of the underlying symptom dynamics.

text.text: Yet the few observed changes were not confined to depressive symptoms, supporting the clinical relevance of considering anxiety symptoms in patients treated for depression. 26 Finally, some change estimates were imprecise, with wide credibility intervals limiting distinction between small treatment-related changes and estimation uncertainty.

text.text: A larger sample may have improved precision of these estimates.

Findings from this intensive short-term treatment invite a broader view of treatment success beyond symptom severity and global connectivity, including activation tendency, specific interaction patterns, and their stability over time.
The observed pattern may reflect greater change in activation tendency than in temporal interaction structure, potentially indicating residual vulnerability.

For the network theory, the limited support for reduced connectivity highlights the need to define more clearly what characterizes a healthy symptom system and how activation tendency and symptom interactions independently or jointly relate to sustained improvement.

Research across assessment timescales, treatment durations, intensities, and settings should determine whether short-term improvement without detectable network restructuring reflects sustained recovery or heightened relapse risk, ultimately informing decisions about treatment duration and continuation of care.

Absolute strength reflects the overall magnitude of interactions, regardless of direction (valence-ignorant), while raw strength retains the direction of effects (valence-sensitive), allowing positive and negative interactions to cancel each other out.
